# Jacob Spon, *Miscellanea eruditae antiquitatis* (1685)

Primary-source pointer for the butterfly/soul iconography used in the LP1 p16 / LP2 p22 source investigation.

- Internet Archive scan: https://archive.org/details/gri_33125008544963
- Wikimedia Commons PDF record: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Miscellanea_eruditae_antiquitatis_-_in_quibus_marmora,_statuae,_musiva,_toreumata,_gemmae,_numismata,_Grutero,_Vrsino,_Boissardo_(IA_gri_33125008544963).pdf
- Contents entry: Art. III, “Nuptiae Cupidinis & Psyches, Papilio animae symbolum”, printed p. 7.

The page-7 plate contains numbered figures III–IX. Spon's Table III commentary describes the butterfly's repeated metamorphosis from worm to butterfly. For Table IV he writes: “Papilio igitur hic expressus viri defuncti anima est quae avolat” (the butterfly depicted here is the soul of the deceased man, which flies away). Table V describes a bird catching the butterfly as a figure of the passage of souls from human bodies into animals. Table VI describes Cupid fastening the soul to a tree with a nail so it cannot ascend. These are the source's iconographic explanations, not cryptographic instructions.

The LP1 p16 image shows a cicada-like insect above a reclining corpse; this is a plausible thematic adaptation of Table IV's butterfly-as-departing-soul motif, not an exact species or crop match. LP2 p22 has a different horizontal object above a corpse and is not claimed as a reuse of the Table IV image. The neighboring original LP1 images add a possible sequence: file 14 shows the corpse alone, file 15 shows two cicada-like insects above it, and file 16 shows one. This is compatible with (but does not prove) an allusion to Spon's adjacent Table III (Cupid/Psyche union) and Table IV (the single departing soul). The source's page7/tableIV numbers are not by themselves a native LP2 page address: the original 2014 Stage11 index numbers its 58 LP2 images 0–57. Do not infer a missing page75 from concatenating 7 and V.

Use the scan as a historical reference. This note does not claim a pixel-verified crop lineage.
